questions.question: After the fall of the Guptas, different kingdoms emerged in various parts of India. Among them, the Maukharis emerged in which of the following areas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kannauj**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Maukharis were an ancient Indian dynasty that ruled over parts of northern India after the decline of the Gupta Empire.
 
• They initially served as vassals of the Guptas before establishing their independent rule.
 
• The Maukharis made Kannauj their capital, which later became a prominent center of power and culture in northern India.
 
• Kannauj, under the Maukharis, became an important political, economic, and cultural hub during their reign.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Maukharis Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Maukharis were initially feudatories of the Guptas but later established their own independent rule in northern India.
 
• They ruled over the region that includes parts of present-day Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
 
• Key rulers of the Maukhari dynasty include Hari-varman and Aditya-varman.
 
 
 
• **Kannauj:**
 
 
• Kannauj is an ancient city in Uttar Pradesh, known for its historical and cultural significance.
 
• It became a major center of power during the rule of various dynasties, including the Maukharis, Harshavardhanas, and the Gurjara-Pratiharas.
 
• During the medieval period, Kannauj was a key battleground for dominance over northern India.
 
 
 
• **Gupta Empire:**
 
 
• The Gupta Empire was one of the largest and most powerful empires in ancient India, known for its advancements in arts, science, and political administration.
 
• It existed approximately from the 4th to the 6th century CE and is often referred to as the Golden Age of India.
 
• Key rulers include Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, and Chandragupta II.

questions.question: Which of the following nations won the ICC World Test Championship, defeating India, in 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Australia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Australia won the ICC World Test Championship in 2023, defeating India in the final match.
 
• The final match was held at The Oval in London from June 7 to June 11, 2023.
 
• This victory marked Australia's first ICC World Test Championship title since the tournament's inception.
 
• Australia's team displayed remarkable performance throughout the tournament, leading to their well-deserved win.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **ICC World Test Championship**

 
 
• The ICC World Test Championship (WTC) is a league competition for Test cricket run by the International Cricket Council (ICC).
 
• The championship was introduced to bring more context and excitement to Test cricket, which is the longest format of the sport.
 
• The WTC started in 2019, with the final match determining the world champion in Test cricket.
 
• The competition involves the top Test-playing nations, with each series contributing points towards the championship table.
 
 
 
• **Final Match Details**
 
 
• The final match of the 2023 ICC World Test Championship was held at The Oval, a historic cricket ground in London, England.
 
• Australia faced India in the final, showcasing top-notch cricketing skills from both sides.
 
• Australia emerged victorious, securing their first WTC title and adding another prestigious trophy to their cricketing achievements.
 
 
 
• **Australia's Cricket Achievements**
 
 
• Australia has a rich history in cricket, being one of the most successful teams in the sport.
 
• They have won multiple ICC Cricket World Cups, ICC Champions Trophies, and now the ICC World Test Championship.
 
• Australia is known for producing legendary cricketers and maintaining a high standard of performance in international cricket.

questions.question: Presently, which of the following countries is NOT a beneficiary of India's Duty-Free Tariff Preference (DFTP) Scheme?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Angola**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Duty-Free Tariff Preference (DFTP) Scheme was introduced by the Government of India in 2008.
 
• The scheme aims to provide market access at zero duty to products originating from Least Developed Countries (LDCs).
 
• Rwanda, Burundi, and Myanmar are some of the beneficiaries of the DFTP Scheme.
 
• Angola is currently not a beneficiary of India's Duty-Free Tariff Preference (DFTP) Scheme.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Duty-Free Tariff Preference (DFTP) Scheme**

 
 
• The DFTP Scheme was launched by India to provide preferential market access for goods originating from Least Developed Countries (LDCs).
 
• The main objective is to enhance South-South cooperation and contribute to the development of LDCs.
 
• The scheme covers around 98% of tariff lines, making a wide range of products from LDCs eligible for zero-duty benefits.
 
• It has the potential to significantly boost exports from LDCs to India, thereby supporting their economic growth and development.
 
 
 
• **Least Developed Countries (LDCs)**
 
 
• LDCs are a group of countries that are recognized by the United Nations as being the most disadvantaged in terms of their low gross national income, weak human assets, and economic vulnerability.
 
• As of October 2023, there are 46 countries classified as LDCs.
 
• LDCs benefit from various international support measures, including preferential market access and development assistance.
 
• The aim is to help these countries overcome structural challenges, eradicate poverty, and achieve sustainable development.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles deals with the composition of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 80**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 80 of the Indian Constitution deals with the composition of the Council of States, which is commonly known as the Rajya Sabha.
 
• The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Parliament of India.
 
• As per Article 80, the Rajya Sabha consists of not more than 250 members.
 
• Out of these, 12 members are nominated by the President of India from among persons having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, science, art, and social service, and the remaining members are representatives of the States and Union territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 76**

 
 
• Article 76 of the Indian Constitution deals with the office of the Attorney General of India.
 
• The Attorney General is the chief legal advisor to the Government of India and has the right to participate in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament, but without a right to vote.
 
 
 
• **Article 84**
 
 
• Article 84 of the Indian Constitution specifies the qualifications required to be a member of Parliament.
 
• These qualifications include being a citizen of India, being not less than 30 years of age in the case of the Rajya Sabha and 25 years in the case of the Lok Sabha, and possessing such other qualifications as may be prescribed by law by the Parliament.
 
 
 
• **Article 92**
 
 
• Article 92 of the Indian Constitution deals with the provisions for the Chairman or Deputy Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).
 
• It states that while the office of Chairman or Deputy Chairman is vacant, or in the absence of the Chairman from any sitting of the Council, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman, or if the Deputy Chairman is also absent, by such member of the Council as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Council.

questions.question: The birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi is celebrated as the national festival of India. In which of the following years was Gandhi Ji born?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1869**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi** was born on **2nd October 1869**.
 
• His full name was **Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi**.
 
• Gandhi is widely recognized as the **Father of the Nation** in India.
 
• He played a key role in **India's independence movement** against British rule through his philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Festivals of India**

 
 
• India celebrates three national festivals: **Republic Day** (26th January), **Independence Day** (15th August), and **Gandhi Jayanti** (2nd October).
 
• Gandhi Jayanti is observed to commemorate the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• On this day, various events and activities are organized across the country to honor his contributions and teachings.
 
• It is also celebrated as the **International Day of Non-Violence** by the United Nations.
 
 
 
• **Philosophy of Mahatma Gandhi**
 
 
• **Ahimsa**: Non-violence, the principle of not causing harm to any living being.
 
• **Satyagraha**: The policy of passive political resistance, especially that advocated by Mahatma Gandhi against British rule in India.
 
• **Swadeshi**: The focus on self-sufficiency and the use of domestic goods.
 
• **Sarvodaya**: The welfare of all, a concept aiming for the progress and upliftment of all sections of society.
 
 
 
• **Important Events in Gandhi's Life**
 
 
• **Salt March** (1930): A nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly.
 
• **Quit India Movement** (1942): A movement demanding an end to British rule in India.
 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920-22): A mass protest demanding self-governance and full independence.
 
• **Assassination**: Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30th January 1948 by Nathuram Godse.

questions.question: What kind of phyllotaxy was examined in the Guava plant?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Opposite**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In an opposite phyllotaxy, two leaves arise at the same level from opposite sides of the stem.
 
• Each pair of leaves is typically perpendicular to the next pair above or below, providing a crisscross pattern.
 
• Opposite phyllotaxy ensures maximum light exposure for each leaf, which is beneficial for photosynthesis.
 
• This type of leaf arrangement is common in plants such as guava (Psidium guajava), calotropis, and jamun.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Phyllotaxy**

 
 
• Phyllotaxy refers to the arrangement of leaves on a plant stem.
 
• The primary types of phyllotaxy are alternate, opposite, and whorled.
 
• This arrangement plays a significant role in maximizing light capture and minimizing shading of lower leaves.
 
 
 
• **Alternate Phyllotaxy**
 
 
• In alternate phyllotaxy, each leaf arises at a different level on the stem, and the leaves are not directly opposite each other.
 
• Examples include sunflower and mustard.
 
 
 
• **Whorled Phyllotaxy**
 
 
• In whorled phyllotaxy, three or more leaves grow at the same level around the stem.
 
• This arrangement is less common and can be seen in plants like Nerium (oleander).

questions.question: The Nandi Award for Best Male Playback Singer was instituted by which state in the year 1977?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andhra Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Nandi Awards are the highest awards given for excellence in Telugu cinema, theatre, and television, presented annually by the Government of Andhra Pradesh.
 
• The awards were instituted in 1964 and have been presented annually ever since.
 
• The Nandi Award for Best Male Playback Singer was instituted in the year 1977.
 
• The awards are named after the big granite bull at Lepakshi, a cultural and historical symbol of the Telugu people.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Telugu Cinema**

 
 
• Telugu cinema, also known as Tollywood, is a part of Indian cinema producing films in the Telugu language.
 
• It is based in Film Nagar, a neighborhood of Hyderabad, Telangana.
 
• Telugu cinema is one of the largest film industries in India and produces a significant number of films annually.
 
 
 
• **Andhra Pradesh**
 
 
• Andhra Pradesh is a state in the southeastern coastal region of India.
 
• It is the seventh-largest state by area and the tenth-most populous state in India.
 
• The state has a rich cultural heritage and is known for its classical dance Kuchipudi and numerous historical monuments and temples.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Film Awards**
 
 
• **National Film Awards:** Established in 1954, these are the most prominent film awards in India that honor the best of Indian cinema on a national level.
 
• **Filmfare Awards:** These are one of the oldest and most prestigious film awards in India, presented annually by The Times Group to honor artistic and technical excellence in the Hindi language film industry.
 
• **IIFA Awards:** The International Indian Film Academy Awards are presented annually by the International Indian Film Academy to honor artistic and technical excellence in Bollywood.

questions.question: Indian Olympic Association was established in which of the following years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1927**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) was established in 1927.
 
• The IOA is the body responsible for selecting athletes to represent India at the Olympic Games, Asian Games, and other international athletic meets.
 
• Sir Dorabji Tata and Dr. A.G. Noehren were the founding members of the IOA.
 
• The IOA is affiliated with the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the Olympic Council of Asia.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Olympic Games**

 
 
• The Olympic Games are leading international sporting events featuring summer and winter sports competitions.
 
• The games are held every four years, with the Summer and Winter Games alternating every two years.
 
• The modern Olympic Games were first held in 1896 in Athens, Greece.
 
• The International Olympic Committee (IOC), established in 1894, is the governing body of the Olympic Movement.
 
 
 
• **Asian Games**
 
 
• The Asian Games, also known as Asiad, is a continental multi-sport event held every four years among athletes from all over Asia.
 
• The Games are regulated by the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) under the supervision of the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
 
• The first Asian Games were held in New Delhi, India, in 1951.
 
 
 
• **International Olympic Committee (IOC)**
 
 
• The International Olympic Committee is a non-governmental sports organization based in Lausanne, Switzerland.
 
• The IOC is the authority responsible for organizing the modern Olympic Games.
 
• It was founded by Pierre de Coubertin and Demetrios Vikelas in 1894.

questions.question: Which of the following is a public sector industry?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**BHEL**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL)** is an Indian public sector engineering and manufacturing company.
 
• It is owned by the Government of India and was established in 1964.
 
• BHEL is one of the largest engineering and manufacturing companies of its kind in India.
 
• The company is engaged in the design, engineering, construction, testing, commissioning, and servicing of a wide range of products and services for the core sectors of the economy, viz. Power, Transmission, Industry, Transportation (Railways), Renewable Energy, Oil & Gas, and Defence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reliance Industries Limited**

 
 
• It is a private sector company and one of the largest conglomerates in India.
 
• Founded by Dhirubhai Ambani in 1966, it is involved in various sectors including petrochemicals, refining, oil, telecommunications, and retail.
 
 
 
• **Tata Group**
 
 
• It is an Indian multinational conglomerate founded in 1868 by Jamsetji Tata.
 
• While it operates in many sectors including steel, automobiles, IT, and hotels, it is a private sector entity.
 
 
 
• **Adani Group**
 
 
• Founded by Gautam Adani in 1988, it is an Indian multinational conglomerate.
 
• It operates in sectors such as energy, resources, logistics, agribusiness, real estate, financial services, and defense.
 
• It is a private sector company.
 
 

This code provides a detailed explanation for the question, including key points about the correct option (BHEL) and additional information about the other options

questions.question: Which of following is NOT a device of parliamentary proceedings?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Full-day discussion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Full-day discussion** is not a recognized device of parliamentary proceedings in India.
 
• Indian Parliament has specific mechanisms for discussions such as **Half-an-hour discussion**, **Zero-hour discussion**, and **Two-hour (short) discussion**.
 
• These mechanisms are structured to ensure organized and efficient proceedings within the Parliament.
 
• The concept of a "Full-day discussion" does not exist as a formal parliamentary procedure in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Half-an-hour discussion**

 
 
• It is a device in the Indian Parliament where members can raise a matter of public importance, which requires an oral answer from the concerned minister.
 
• This discussion takes place for half an hour, typically at the end of the day's session.
 
• It allows members to seek clarification on specific issues from the ministers.
 
 
 
• **Zero-hour discussion**
 
 
• It is an informal device available to the members of the Indian Parliament to raise matters without any prior notice.
 
• It starts immediately after the Question Hour and lasts until the agenda for the day is taken up.
 
• Members can raise urgent matters of public importance during this time.
 
 
 
• **Two-hour (short) discussion**
 
 
• This device allows for a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for a duration of two hours.
 
• No formal motion is moved and no voting takes place at the end of the discussion.
 
• The aim is to allow members to express their views and enable the government to clarify its position on the issue.

questions.question: Which of the following rivers marks the eastern-most boundary of the Himalayas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Brahmaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Brahmaputra river originates from the Angsi Glacier in the Himalayas in Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo River.
 
• It flows eastwards for about 1,700 km through the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, making a U-turn at the Namcha Barwa mountain to enter India in Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• The river marks the eastern-most boundary of the Himalayas, after which it turns southward into the Assam Valley as the Brahmaputra and further into Bangladesh.
 
• The Brahmaputra is one of the major rivers of the Indian subcontinent, with a total length of 2,900 km, making it one of the longest rivers in the world.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kali River**

 
 
• The Kali River, also known as the Sharda River or Mahakali River, flows along the border of India and Nepal.
 
• It originates from the Kalapani springs in the Himalayas at an altitude of 3,600 meters in the Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand, India.
 
• The river is significant for both nations, serving as a vital water resource and playing a role in the bilateral treaties between India and Nepal.
 
 
 
• **Teesta River**
 
 
• Teesta River originates from the Tso Lhamo Lake in North Sikkim, India, and flows southward through West Bengal before entering Bangladesh.
 
• It is a major river in the Indian states of Sikkim and West Bengal, providing water for irrigation and hydroelectric power generation.
 
 
 
• **Satluj River**
 
 
• The Satluj River, also known as the Sutlej, is the longest of the five rivers that flow through the Punjab region in northern India and Pakistan.
 
• It originates in Tibet near Lake Rakshastal and flows through the Indian states of Himachal Pradesh and Punjab before entering Pakistan.

questions.question: What is the empirically fitted relationship between the rate of change of money, wage, and rate of unemployment known as?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Philips curve**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Philips curve represents the inverse relationship between the rate of unemployment and the rate of inflation in an economy.
 
• The concept was first introduced by economist A.W. Phillips in 1958.
 
• According to the Phillips curve, lower unemployment in an economy leads to higher wages, which in turn leads to higher inflation.
 
• This relationship suggests that policymakers face a trade-off between reducing unemployment and controlling inflation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Friedman's Model**

 
 
• Also known as the Monetarist Theory, it was proposed by Milton Friedman.
 
• Friedman argued that there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, as suggested by the Phillips curve.
 
• He introduced the concept of the Natural Rate of Unemployment, which posits that the economy will always revert to this natural rate despite short-term fluctuations.
 
• Friedman emphasized the role of monetary policy in controlling inflation.
 
 
 
• **Keynesian Model**
 
 
• Developed by John Maynard Keynes, this model emphasizes total spending in the economy (aggregate demand) and its effects on output and inflation.
 
• Keynesians advocate for active government intervention to manage economic cycles.
 
• They believe that insufficient demand can lead to prolonged periods of high unemployment.
 
• In contrast to the Phillips curve, Keynesians may support policies that increase aggregate demand to reduce unemployment without necessarily causing high inflation.
 
 
 
• **Baumol Hypothesis**
 
 
• Proposed by economist William J. Baumol, it addresses the cost disease in service sectors.
 
• Baumol's hypothesis suggests that wages in labor-intensive sectors (like services) rise due to wage increases in other sectors that experience higher productivity growth.
 
• This leads to higher costs in the service sector without corresponding increases in productivity.
 
• The hypothesis is often used to explain rising costs in sectors such as healthcare and education.

questions.question: Which of the following is India's national academy of dance?

options.text: Centre for Cultural Resources and Training

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sangeet Natak Akademi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sangeet Natak Akademi** is the national level academy for performing arts in India, including dance, music, and drama.
 
• It was established by the Indian Education Ministry in 1952 and is an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Culture.
 
• The Akademi's primary goal is to promote and preserve the rich and diverse cultural heritage of India in the field of performing arts.
 
• It recognizes and honors outstanding artists through its annual awards and fellowships, which are considered the highest national recognition given to artists.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lalit Kala Akademi**

 
 
• Also known as the National Academy of Art, it is India's national academy of fine arts.
 
• It was established in New Delhi in 1954 by the Government of India to promote and propagate understanding of Indian art, both within and outside the country.
 
• The Akademi organizes exhibitions, workshops, and seminars to foster a deeper appreciation of various forms of visual arts.
 
 
 
• **Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT)**
 
 
• CCRT is an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Culture, Government of India.
 
• Established in 1979, the CCRT's primary objective is to link education with culture and to promote the integration of cultural knowledge in the school education system.
 
• CCRT conducts training programs, workshops, and provides resources for teachers and students to promote cultural education.
 
 
 
• **Centre for Indian Classical Dances**
 
 
• Founded by the renowned classical dancer Dr. Sonal Mansingh in 1977, it is dedicated to the preservation and promotion of Indian classical dance forms.
 
• The center offers training and educational programs in various classical dance styles such as Bharatanatyam, Odissi, and others.
 
• It aims to maintain the traditional standards of Indian classical dances while encouraging innovation and creativity.

questions.question: Padma Bhushan awardee, Ustad Sabri Khan played which of the following musical instruments?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sarangi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Ustad Sabri Khan was a renowned Sarangi player, known for his contributions to Indian classical music.
 
• He received the Padma Bhushan award in 2006, one of India's highest civilian honors, for his exceptional service in the field of arts.
 
• Ustad Sabri Khan played a significant role in popularizing the Sarangi on an international level.
 
• He belonged to the Sainia Gharana, which traces its roots back to Mian Tansen, one of the greatest musicians in Indian history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sarangi**

 
 
• The Sarangi is a bowed, short-necked string instrument from India, which is used in Hindustani classical music.
 
• It is known for its emotive and vocal quality, often compared to the human voice.
 
• The Sarangi has three main playing strings made of gut and a number of sympathetic strings that resonate with the played notes, providing a rich, echoing sound.
 
• It is traditionally played using a bow and is held vertically, resting on the knee of the musician.
 
 
 
• **Sarod**
 
 
• The Sarod is another stringed instrument used in Indian classical music, known for its deep, weighty, and introspective sound.
 
• It is played with a plectrum and has a fretless metal fingerboard, allowing for smooth sliding movements.
 
• The Sarod has a wooden body with a resonating membrane made of goat skin, and it usually has four to six main strings and numerous sympathetic strings.
 
 
 
• **Santoor**
 
 
• The Santoor is a hammered dulcimer from the Kashmir region, played with lightweight wooden mallets called mezrab.
 
• It has a trapezoid shape and is usually made of walnut or maple wood, with a total of 72 strings arranged in sets of three, producing a bright, shimmering sound.
 
• The instrument is placed on the lap and played while sitting cross-legged, and it is used in both classical and folk music.
 
 
 
• **Tabla**
 
 
• The Tabla is a pair of twin hand drums used in Indian classical, popular, and devotional music.
 
• Consisting of a smaller drum called 'dayan' (right) and a larger drum called 'bayan' (left), the Tabla is known for its complex rhythms and tonal versatility.
 
• It is played with the fingers and palms, allowing for a wide range of dynamic and expressive sounds.

questions.question: Transition elements are the elements that are found in Groups 3-12 of the modern periodic table, that constitute the ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**d-block**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Transition elements are the elements that are found in the d-block of the periodic table.
 
• The d-block elements are located in Groups 3 to 12 of the periodic table.
 
• These elements are characterized by the filling of d-orbitals in their electron configuration.
 
• Transition elements exhibit unique properties such as variable oxidation states, colored compounds, and catalytic properties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Periodic Table:**

 
 
• The periodic table is an arrangement of chemical elements organized based on their atomic number, electron configuration, and recurring chemical properties.
 
• Elements are presented in order of increasing atomic number.
 
• The table is divided into several blocks: s-block, p-block, d-block, and f-block, based on the subshell in which the last electron resides.
 
 
 
• **d-block Elements:**
 
 
• d-block elements are also known as transition metals.
 
• These elements have partially filled d-orbitals in their ground state or in any of their oxidation states.
 
• Common properties of d-block elements include high melting and boiling points, formation of colored compounds, and the ability to form complex ions.
 
• Examples of d-block elements include iron (Fe), copper (Cu), and nickel (Ni).
 
 
 
• **s-block Elements:**
 
 
• s-block elements include groups 1 and 2 of the periodic table, which comprise alkali metals and alkaline earth metals.
 
• These elements have their outermost electron in an s-orbital.
 
• Examples include lithium (Li), sodium (Na), and calcium (Ca).
 
 
 
• **p-block Elements:**
 
 
• p-block elements are found in groups 13-18 of the periodic table.
 
• These elements have their outermost electrons in p-orbitals.
 
• Examples include carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and oxygen (O).
 
 
 
• **f-block Elements:**
 
 
• f-block elements include the lanthanides and actinides.
 
• These elements have their outermost electrons in f-orbitals.
 
• Examples include cerium (Ce), thorium (Th), and uranium (U).

questions.question: A small object is placed on the focus on the left side of a convex lens. Where will the image be formed?

options.text: At the centre on the right side of the lens.
At infinity on the left side of the lens.
At infinity on the right side of the lens.
At the focus on the right side of the lens.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**At infinity on the right side of the lens**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When an object is placed at the focus of a convex lens, the rays after refraction through the lens become parallel to each other.
 
• Parallel rays are considered to meet at infinity on the other side of the lens.
 
• Thus, the image formed will be at infinity on the right side of the lens.
 
• This image will be highly enlarged and real.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Convex Lens:**

 
 
• A convex lens is thicker at the center than at the edges and is also known as a converging lens because it converges light rays that are initially parallel.
 
• It is used in various optical devices such as magnifying glasses, cameras, and corrective lenses for farsightedness.
 
 
 
• **Focus:**
 
 
• The focus (or focal point) of a lens is the point where parallel light rays converge (for a convex lens) or appear to diverge from (for a concave lens).
 
• The distance from the lens to the focus is called the focal length.
 
 
 
• **Image Formation by Convex Lens:**
 
 
• When an object is placed at the focus of a convex lens, the refracted rays become parallel, indicating that the image is formed at infinity.
 
• When the object is placed between the lens and the focus, the image formed is virtual, erect, and enlarged.

questions.question: One of the greatest of Chola ruler Rajaraja I ruled from 985 AD to ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1014 AD**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Rajaraja I was one of the most significant and powerful rulers of the Chola dynasty, which ruled Southern India.
 
• He ruled from 985 AD to 1014 AD, marking a period of great expansion and consolidation of the Chola Empire.
 
• During his reign, the Chola Empire expanded its territories to include parts of present-day Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, and Sri Lanka.
 
• Rajaraja I is known for his administrative prowess, military conquests, and contributions to art and architecture, including the construction of the famous Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chola Dynasty**

 
 
• The Chola dynasty was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in the history of southern India, with its roots tracing back to the early centuries CE.
 
• It reached its zenith under the rule of Rajaraja I and his successors, who expanded the empire significantly.
 
• The Cholas were known for their naval prowess and had a strong maritime influence, establishing trade links with Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.
 
• The Chola period is often regarded as a golden age of Tamil culture and literature, with significant contributions to art, architecture, and temple building.
 
 
 
• **Brihadeeswarar Temple**
 
 
• The Brihadeeswarar Temple, also known as the Big Temple, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Shiva, located in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu.
 
• It was built by Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 AD and is considered a masterpiece of Dravidian architecture.
 
• The temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is renowned for its grandeur, intricate carvings, and massive proportions.
 
• The temple's Vimana (tower) is one of the tallest in the world, standing at around 66 meters (216 feet).
 
 
 
• **Rajaraja I**
 
 
• Rajaraja I was born as Arulmozhivarman, and he ascended the throne as Rajaraja Chola I in 985 AD.
 
• He is known for his military conquests, which included the annexation of the Pandya and Chera territories and the northern part of Sri Lanka.
 
• Rajaraja I reformed the administrative system of the Chola Empire, improving revenue collection and enhancing the efficiency of governance.
 
• He is also credited with initiating the construction of the Brihadeeswarar Temple, which stands as a testament to his patronage of art and architecture.
 
 

This source code provides a detailed explanation of the correct answer along with key points and additional information related to the Chola dynasty, Rajaraja I, and the Brihadeeswarar Temple

questions.question: Who asked James Rennel to prepare the map of Hindustan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Robert Clive**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Robert Clive** was a British officer and privateer who established the military and political supremacy of the East India Company in Bengal.
 
• He is credited with helping to establish British control over India, which lasted until Indian independence in 1947.
 
• James Rennel, a geographer and historian, was asked by Robert Clive to prepare a map of Hindustan.
 
• Rennel's map was one of the earliest detailed maps of India, and it played a significant role in the British administration and strategic planning in the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **James Rennel**

 
 
• James Rennel (1742-1830) was an English geographer, historian, and pioneer of oceanography.
 
• He is often referred to as the Father of Indian Geography for his extensive surveys and maps of the Indian subcontinent.
 
• His work provided critical geographical information that was used for military and administrative purposes by the British Empire.
 
• Rennel's most notable work, "A Bengal Atlas," was published in 1779 and included detailed maps of Bengal and parts of Northern India.
 
 
 
• **Robert Clive**
 
 
• Robert Clive (1725-1774) was a British military officer and a key figure in establishing British control in India.
 
• He played a crucial role in the Battle of Plassey (1757), which marked the beginning of British rule in India.
 
• Clive served as the Governor of Bengal and implemented significant administrative reforms to strengthen British power.
 
• Despite his achievements, Clive's career was marred by controversies, including allegations of corruption and his role in the exploitation of Indian resources.
 
 
 
• **East India Company**
 
 
• The East India Company was an English company formed for the exploitation of trade with East and Southeast Asia and India, incorporated by royal charter in 1600.
 
• The company eventually came to rule large areas of India, exercising military power and assuming administrative functions.
 
• It played a key role in the British colonization of India and its economy was heavily reliant on the trade of cotton, silk, indigo, salt, tea, and opium.
 
• The company's rule in India ended after the Indian Rebellion of 1857, leading to the establishment of direct British rule, known as the British Raj.

questions.question: Who among the following is appointed as the new Chairman of Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) in March 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Deepak Mohanty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Deepak Mohanty was appointed as the new Chairman of the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) in March 2023.
 
• He succeeded Supratim Bandyopadhyay, who served as the previous chairman of PFRDA.
 
• Deepak Mohanty has previously held the position of Executive Director at the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
 
• PFRDA is the regulatory body for overseeing and promoting the pension sector in India, including the National Pension System (NPS).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA)**

 
 
• The PFRDA was established by the Government of India to promote, regulate, and develop the pension sector in India.
 
• It was set up on 23 August 2003 and became a statutory body with the enactment of the PFRDA Act in 2013.
 
• The PFRDA oversees and regulates the National Pension System (NPS) and other pension schemes to ensure that the retirement needs of individuals are met effectively.
 
• The NPS is a voluntary, defined contribution retirement savings scheme designed to enable subscribers to make decisions regarding their future through systematic savings during their working life.
 
 
 
• **National Pension System (NPS)**
 
 
• The NPS is a government-sponsored pension scheme launched in January 2004 for government employees and later extended to all citizens of India.
 
• It is a voluntary and long-term retirement savings scheme aimed at ensuring that subscribers receive a stable income post-retirement.
 
• Under NPS, individual savings are pooled into a pension fund which is invested by PFRDA-regulated professional fund managers as per approved investment guidelines into diversified portfolios comprising government bonds, bills, corporate debentures, and shares.
 
• The NPS offers tax benefits under Section 80CCD of the Income Tax Act, making it an attractive investment option for retirement planning.
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**
 
 
• The RBI is India's central banking institution, which controls the issuance and supply of the Indian rupee and manages the country's main payment systems.
 
• It was established on April 1, 1935, in accordance with the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
 
• The RBI plays a crucial role in the development strategy of the Indian government, focusing on economic growth and stability.
 
• In addition to its primary functions, the RBI manages foreign exchange and gold reserves, regulates the financial system, and provides key financial services to the government and the banking sector.

questions.question: Indian National Army was formed in which of the following countries?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Singapore**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian National Army (INA) was formed during World War II in Singapore.
 
• The INA was initially formed under the leadership of Mohan Singh in 1942 with the aim of securing Indian independence from British rule.
 
• It was later reorganized and led by Subhas Chandra Bose, who took command in 1943.
 
• Singapore served as a strategic location for the INA due to its significant Indian population and its occupation by the Japanese forces at the time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Army (INA)**

 
 
• The Indian National Army (INA) was an armed force formed by Indian nationalists in 1942 in Southeast Asia during World War II.
 
• The aim of the INA was to secure Indian independence from British rule, a cause that garnered significant support among Indian expatriates and prisoners of war.
 
• Mohan Singh initially formed the INA with Indian prisoners of war captured by the Japanese during the Malayan Campaign and the Battle of Singapore.
 
• Subhas Chandra Bose, a prominent leader in the Indian independence movement, took charge of the INA in 1943 and restructured it significantly.
 
 
 
• **Subhas Chandra Bose**
 
 
• Subhas Chandra Bose, also known as Netaji, was a prominent Indian freedom fighter who played a crucial role in the Indian independence movement.
 
• Bose was a charismatic leader who advocated for radical action against British rule and sought foreign alliances to achieve Indian independence.
 
• Under his leadership, the INA sought to liberate India from British control with the assistance of the Axis powers during World War II.
 
• Bose's efforts and his call for complete independence inspired many Indians and left a lasting legacy in India's history.
 
 
 
• **World War II and Southeast Asia**
 
 
• World War II, which lasted from 1939 to 1945, involved major global powers and was marked by significant military campaigns in various regions, including Southeast Asia.
 
• Southeast Asia was strategically important during the war, with countries like Singapore, Malaya, and Burma witnessing major battles.
 
• The Japanese occupation of Southeast Asia during the war provided an opportunity for Indian nationalists to seek support for their cause against British colonial rule.
 
• The INA's formation and activities in Southeast Asia were part of the broader context of anti-colonial struggles and the global impact of World War II.

questions.question: Which Article in the fundamental duty applies, when a construction worker takes his 8-year son to the site rather than sending him to school?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 51A (k)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 51A (k) of the Constitution of India** specifies that it is a fundamental duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between the ages of 6 and 14 years.
 
• This duty is in line with the objective of the Right to Education Act, which mandates free and compulsory education for children in this age group.
 
• Ensuring that children go to school instead of being involved in child labor is essential for their overall development and future prospects.
 
• Violation of this duty, such as taking a child to a construction site instead of school, can lead to legal consequences and hinder the child's right to education.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties**

 
 
• Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations specified in Part IVA (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976, based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• These duties emphasize the importance of citizen participation in national development and the upholding of constitutional values.
 
 
 
• **Right to Education Act (RTE)**
 
 
• The Right to Education Act was enacted in 2009 to provide free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• It is a fundamental right under Article 21A of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Act ensures that children have access to quality education without discrimination and establishes norms for school infrastructure, teacher-student ratio, and curriculum.
 
 
 
• **Child Labor**
 
 
• Child labor refers to the employment of children in a manner that deprives them of their childhood, education, or is harmful to their health and development.
 
• The Child Labor (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, and its amendments prohibit the employment of children below 14 years in hazardous occupations and processes.
 
• Efforts to eliminate child labor involve providing education and support to families to ensure children attend school instead of engaging in work.
 
 

This source code provides a detailed solution to the question regarding the fundamental duty applicable when a construction worker takes his 8-year-old son to the site instead of sending him to school. The key points highlight the importance and implications of Article 51A (k), while the additional information section provides context on related topics such as Fundamental Duties, the Right to Education Act, and child labor

questions.question: Exfoliation is a form of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**physical weathering**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Exfoliation is a type of physical weathering that involves the peeling away of layers of rock.
 
• This process often occurs in areas with significant temperature fluctuations, causing the rock to expand and contract.
 
• Over time, the stress from temperature changes leads to the separation of the outer layers of the rock.
 
• Exfoliation can be observed in large rock formations, especially in mountainous regions and granite domes.

 [IMAGE: https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcSz_Lu9-Mx-xDK8yOTgMd2LZez7aitby_B1fw&s] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Physical Weathering:**

 
 
• It is the process of breaking down rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition.
 
• Common agents of physical weathering include temperature changes, frost action, and the activity of living organisms.
 
• Examples of physical weathering processes include freeze-thaw cycles, exfoliation, and abrasion.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Weathering:**
 
 
• It involves the chemical alteration of minerals within the rock, leading to its breakdown.
 
• Common agents include water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and various acids.
 
• Examples include oxidation, hydrolysis, and carbonation.
 
 
 
• **Mass Wasting:**
 
 
• It refers to the downslope movement of soil and rock under the influence of gravity.
 
• Examples include landslides, rockfalls, and soil creep.
 
 
 
• **Biochemical Weathering:**
 
 
• It is the breakdown of rocks through the chemical and physical actions of organisms.
 
• Examples include the production of organic acids by plant roots and the burrowing activities of animals.

questions.question: Which Bill was passed by the Parliament, in July 2021, to help in the availability of working capital for the micro, small and medium enterprises sector?

options.text: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2021

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Factoring Regulation (Amendment) Bill, 2021**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Factoring Regulation (Amendment) Bill, 2021 was introduced to address the challenges faced by the micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in accessing working capital.
 
• Factoring is a financial transaction where a business sells its accounts receivable (invoices) to a third party (called a factor) at a discount in exchange for immediate money.
 
• This amendment widens the scope of entities that can undertake factoring business, thereby increasing the availability of funds to the MSME sector.
 
• The Bill aims to simplify the operational constraints in the factoring business and make it more accessible and affordable for MSMEs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Essential Commodities (Amendment) Bill, 2020**

 
 
• This bill aims to deregulate the production, supply, distribution, and trade of certain food items to increase the competitiveness of the market.
 
• It seeks to remove commodities like cereals, pulses, oilseeds, edible oils, onions, and potatoes from the list of essential commodities.
 
• This deregulation is expected to attract private sector/foreign direct investment into the agriculture sector.
 
 
 
• **The Minerals Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2020**
 
 
• This bill aims to promote ease of doing business in the coal and mining sector by amending the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015.
 
• It allows companies to participate in auctions of coal and lignite blocks even without prior experience in coal mining.
 
• The bill also removes the restriction on end-use of minerals produced from coal and lignite blocks.
 
 
 
• **The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2021**
 
 
• This bill introduces a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PIRP) for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
 
• PIRP is a quicker and cost-effective alternative to the normal Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).
 
• This process allows MSMEs to restructure their liabilities and continue their business operations without undergoing a full insolvency process.

questions.question: Identify the structural formula for magnesium hydroxide.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mg(OH)₂**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Magnesium hydroxide has the chemical formula **Mg(OH)2**.
 
• It consists of one magnesium (Mg) atom and two hydroxide (OH) groups.
 
• It is commonly found in nature as the mineral brucite.
 
• Magnesium hydroxide is used as an antacid and a laxative in medicine.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Magnesium (Mg)**

 
 
• Magnesium is a chemical element with the symbol Mg and atomic number 12.
 
• It is a shiny gray solid, and it is the eighth most abundant element in the Earth's crust.
 
• Magnesium is essential for all living cells, playing a key role in various biological processes.
 
 
 
• **Hydroxide (OH-)**
 
 
• The hydroxide ion (OH-) is a diatomic anion consisting of oxygen and hydrogen.
 
• It is commonly found in bases and is responsible for the basic (alkaline) nature of compounds.
 
• Hydroxide ions can neutralize acids, forming water and salts.
 
 
 
• **Magnesium Hydroxide (Mg(OH)2)**
 
 
• Magnesium hydroxide is a white solid with low solubility in water.
 
• It is used in medicine as an antacid to neutralize stomach acid and relieve indigestion and heartburn.
 
• It is also used as a laxative to alleviate constipation.
 
• In industrial applications, magnesium hydroxide is used as a fire retardant and in wastewater treatment.
